chunks: My father (may Allah have mercy on him) and a group of our scholars, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, narrated from Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Maythami, from 'Ali al-Azraq, from al-Hasan ibn al-Hakam al-Nakha'i, from a man who said:

I heard the Commander of the Believers (peace be upon him) in al-Rahbah while he was reciting this verse: 'So neither did the weep over them was the heaven nor the earth, nor were they granted respite.' Then al-Husayn (peace be upon him) came out from one of the doors of the mosque, and he said: 'As for him, verily he will be killed, and the heaven and the earth will weep over him.'

key_terms.فَمَا بَكَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّمَاءُ وَالْ: So neither did the weep over them was the heaven nor the earth

ai.seo_question: What is the connection between Surah Ad-Dukhan verse 29 and the martyrdom of Imam al-Husayn?
ai.summary: This narration from *Kamil al-Ziyarat* establishes a profound theological link between the cosmic grief for Imam al-Husayn and the Quranic description of the heavens and earth not weeping for the disbelievers of Pharaoh's time (Surah Ad-Dukhan 44:29). By contrasting the lack of cosmic mourning for the unjust with the inevitable weeping for the martyr of Karbala, the hadith underscores the unique spiritual status of Ahl al-Bayt in Shia eschatology. It serves as a foundational text for the ritual of weeping, framing it not merely as human emotion but as a reflection of the universe's response to divine justice.
